news_drafts.headline: Scottish Borders forecasts £1.78m education overspend for 2026/27 after £1.735m budget transfers
news_drafts.lead:
Education and Children's Services at Scottish Borders Council is forecasting a net overspend of £1.78m for 2026/27, according to the September revenue monitoring report before the Executive Committee on 10 November. The figure is after temporary transfers of budget from two other services: £0.79m from Finance and £0.86m from Infrastructure and Environment.

Before the transfers, the service's projected outturn variance for the year is £3.517m. The appendix to the report gives the proposed transfer as £1.735m, which leaves the net overspend at £1.781m. The papers attribute the pressure mainly to external placements and Home to School Transport. Underspends in Additional Support Needs partly offset them.

The report also says workforce pressures are adding to costs. It cites absence and maternity cover in schools.

news_drafts.headline: Scottish Borders used its own cash instead of £111.3m of borrowing at March 2026, down from £127.9m
news_drafts.lead:
Scottish Borders Council ended 2025/26 having used its own spare cash, rather than taking out loans, to pay for £111.3m of spending on long-lasting assets such as buildings and roads. A year earlier the figure was £127.9m. The figures are in the council's annual treasury management report (how it borrows, invests spare cash and manages the risks of both), which went to its Audit Committee on 21 September 2026.

The papers measure this against the capital financing requirement, the total the council has spent on long-lived assets that it has not yet paid for, in effect its underlying need to borrow. Using cash in place of a loan is known as internal borrowing, which saves interest but uses up the council's own cushion. The report says the council "has again, where possible, deferred borrowing using surplus cash rather than undertaking new borrowing". It describes this as a deliberate policy and puts the fall in the figure down to lower expected capital demands.

An appendix to the report compares the requirement one year ahead with the council's external debt, the total of all loans it owes. On that basis the council "remains under-borrowed by £65.9m at the end of 2025/26", the paper says.

news_drafts.headline: Scottish Borders pension fund cash deficit widens as pensioners outnumber active members
news_drafts.lead: The Scottish Borders Council pension fund faces a structural cash deficit as pensioner numbers have grown to exceed active member numbers for the first time, with one pensioner now for every active member employed. Over the year to June 2026, pension payments and costs of £366m outstripped contributions by £9m, a shortfall the fund must cover from investment returns and reserves. Pensioner membership has risen 28% over five years while active members grew just 2.9%, a demographic shift that began when the fund matured in 2013/14. This year the fund delivered a 5.7% investment return, the lowest among Scotland's 11 local government pension schemes and well below its 12.3% benchmark; the fund has since terminated underperforming equity managers and committed to changes. Despite the cash flows, Audit Scotland's draft annual report concluded the fund has effective governance and financial management arrangements in place. The council's employer contribution rate was cut to 17% from 18.5% following a strong 134% funding valuation in 2023.

findings.committee: Pension Fund Committee and Pension Board
findings.headline: The Committee approved the proposed appointment of two equity investment managers, subject to completion of satisfactory due diligence.
findings.detail: The item was taken in private, so the paper does not name the managers or the mandates. The approval is conditional on due diligence being completed.
findings.matters: Manager appointments following a selection exercise are the step that moves a fund's allocation from plan to contract, which is what other councils' finance officers compare when reviewing their own selection processes.
findings.quote: The Committee approved the proposed appointment of two equity investment managers, subject to completion of satisfactory due diligence.

findings.committee: Pension Fund Committee and Pension Board
findings.headline: The Pension Fund's net investment assets exceeded £1 billion at the reporting date, with a net withdrawal of approximately £11 million during 2025/26 funded by investment income.
findings.detail: Audit Scotland highlighted the maturing cashflow position, with benefit payments and payments to leavers exceeding contributions and transfers received. The auditor said the Fund remained in a strong overall funding position.
findings.matters: A fund that has moved into net cash outflow and is meeting it from investment income is a position other councils' pension funds will be tracking as they mature.
findings.figures: net investment assets exceeding £1 billion; net withdrawal of approximately £11 million
findings.quote: net investment assets exceeding £1 billion at the reporting date

findings.committee: Pension Fund Committee and Pension Board
findings.headline: Total expenditure to 30 June 2026 was £2.440m, with projected total expenditure of £9.839m for the year to 31 March 2027 against a budget of £9.839m.
findings.detail: This was the first quarterly monitoring report of the budget approved on 5 March 2026. The paper states that at this stage all expenses were in line with the projected budget to 31 March 2027.
findings.matters: A projected outturn equal to budget at the first quarter is the baseline a finance director would check later monitoring reports against.
findings.figures: £2.440m spent to 30 June 2026; £9.839m projected expenditure; £9.839m budget
findings.quote: Total expenditure to 30 June 2026 was £2.440m, with projected total expenditure of £9.839m against a budget of £9.839m.

findings.committee: Pension Fund Committee and Pension Board
findings.headline: M&G is expected to begin drawing down its investment allocation from the beginning of October, with a similar position anticipated for IFM, after the M&G deployment took longer than originally anticipated.
findings.detail: Officers said a number of significant investment movements were expected in the following quarter. Members noted the first M&G drawdown was imminent. The delay was attributed to LGPS governance processes and the investment windows for individual mandates.
findings.matters: Slippage in the timing of private-markets commitments affects cash balances and the timing of the returns they are expected to produce, which matters to any fund planning its drawdowns.
findings.quote: notification had been received that M&G expected to commence drawing down its investment allocation from the beginning of October

findings.committee: Pension Fund Committee and Pension Board
findings.headline: Audit Scotland issued an unmodified audit opinion on the Pension Fund's 2025/26 accounts, with no recommendations for improvement and the 2 prior-year recommendations closed.
findings.detail: The draft Annual Audit Report recorded no significant matters arising, and one small unadjusted difference relating to timing of fund manager confirmations was below materiality. The committee approved the audited Annual Report and Accounts for officer signature and Council approval.
findings.matters: A clean opinion with prior recommendations closed is a measure finance officers at other councils compare against when judging their own pension fund audits.
findings.figures: 2 prior year recommendations closed; no recommendations for improvement
findings.quote: The Scottish Borders Council’s Pension Fund Annual Audit Report 2025/26 highlighted no recommendations for improvement and closed the 2 prior year recommendations.

daily_post.headline: The PWLB 25-year certainty rate rose from 6.20% on 1 April 2026 to 6.67% on 30 September 2026.
daily_post.lead: The cost of long-dated PWLB funding is the number a council weighs against replacing LOBO and maturing debt, so a finance director at another council would want to see the change.
